::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Why vector field $f(x,y)=(y,0)$ is not conservative?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5154532/why-vector-field-fx-y-y-0-is-not-conservative), asked by [Kolkatas](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1781165/kolkatas) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2026-11-17; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I want to check if the vector field $f(x,y)=(y,0)$ is conservative in upper half plane, i.e. $\{(x,y): y>0\}$. 
>
> On desmos.com, the picture of this vector field in the upper half-plane shows horizontal arrows pointing to the right. 
>
> Since there is no circle, I thought that it was conservative. 
>
> But with $P(x,y)=y$ and $Q(x,y)=0$, we see that 
> $$P_y\neq Q_x$$
> at any point in the domain. 
>
> **What is my mistake in understanding?** I am totally confused here myself, due to improper reading on online resources; I trust here the suggestions of experts on this site!
:::

“There is no circle” is too reductive a restatement of the condition that there must be no *rotation* in a conservative vector field. The more precise statement comes from the curl, as you computed. 

But you can still find the circles. Notice
$$f(x,y) = (y/2,x/2) + (y/2,-x/2) = \nabla\left(\frac{xy}{2}\right)+ (y/2,-x/2)$$
So $f$ differs from a circular vector field by a conservative vector field.
